I am writing to submit an application under the provisions of the Freedom of Information Act, 2014. 

My request pertains to certain records related to Approved Housing Bodies (AHBs) and their vacant units in your Council area. 

I would greatly appreciate your assistance in providing the following information.

In response to a recent press query seeking specific data on Approved Housing Bodies, I was informed by the Council’s communications department that there in 2023, there were 16 AHB units that “fall under various categories such as hard to let, works required, legal issues etc.”

With regard to those 16 vacant units, I am hereby requesting the following records:

a. A comprehensive list of the aforementioned units, including their respective addresses and the names of the AHBs responsible for owning/managing each of these units, and the length of time these units have remained vacant as of January 2023.

Please note:

I would like to bring to your attention the 2015 Value-for-Money report on Approved Housing Bodies issued by the Local Government Auditor. 

The report emphasizes the necessity for local authorities to maintain a management information system encompassing details of all properties provided by AHBs, whether purchased, built, or leased units. 

It states:

“The local authorities need to operate a management information system which maintains
details of all properties provided by the AHBs (whether purchased/built or leased units), and
should be agreed periodically with the Department. Details of the tenants of each property,
nomination details, and rent scheme details should also be maintained. The system should
also track details of voids, length of time for re-lets, details of property inspections etc.”

Given this recommendation, I assume that the Council has access to the requested information through its property management system, rendering it eligible for release under section 17(4) of the FOI Act. 

This section mandates FOI bodies to undertake reasonable efforts to search for and extract data, even if a new record is not created.

b. I am also requesting copies of the Annual Statements of Occupancy for each vacant unit covering the years 2020, 2021, and 2022.

Please note: The 2015 Value-for-Money report states that AHBs should submit annual statements of occupancy to the local authorities for all properties funded by the latter. 

The report states:

“It is recommended that an annual statement of occupancy should be submitted by the AHBs to the local authority for all properties funded by the local authorities.”


c. Finally, I seek access to any communications exchanged between the AHBs responsible for owning/managing the aforementioned vacant units, and your Council's Housing Section, that pertain to the vacant units. 

The timeframe I am referring to for these communications is from 2020 to the present.

I kindly request that the information be made available in electronic format.

I am writing to submit an application under the provisions of the Freedom of Information Act, 2014. 

My request pertains to certain records related to Approved Housing Bodies (AHBs) and their vacant units in your Council area. 

I would greatly appreciate your assistance in providing the following information.

In response to a recent press query seeking specific data on Approved Housing Bodies, I was informed by the Council’s communications department that there in 2023, there were 16 AHB units that “fall under various categories such as hard to let, works required, legal issues etc.”

With regard to those 16 vacant units, I am hereby requesting the following records:

a. A comprehensive list of the aforementioned units, including their respective addresses and the names of the AHBs responsible for owning/managing each of these units, and the length of time these units have remained vacant as of January 2023.

Please note:

I would like to bring to your attention the 2015 Value-for-Money report on Approved Housing Bodies issued by the Local Government Auditor. 

The report emphasizes the necessity for local authorities to maintain a management information system encompassing details of all properties provided by AHBs, whether purchased, built, or leased units. 

It states:

“The local authorities need to operate a management information system which maintains
details of all properties provided by the AHBs (whether purchased/built or leased units), and
should be agreed periodically with the Department. Details of the tenants of each property,
nomination details, and rent scheme details should also be maintained. The system should
also track details of voids, length of time for re-lets, details of property inspections etc.”

Given this recommendation, I assume that the Council has access to the requested information through its property management system, rendering it eligible for release under section 17(4) of the FOI Act. 

This section mandates FOI bodies to undertake reasonable efforts to search for and extract data, even if a new record is not created.

b. I am also requesting copies of the Annual Statements of Occupancy for each vacant unit covering the years 2020, 2021, and 2022.

Please note: The 2015 Value-for-Money report states that AHBs should submit annual statements of occupancy to the local authorities for all properties funded by the latter. 

The report states:

“It is recommended that an annual statement of occupancy should be submitted by the AHBs to the local authority for all properties funded by the local authorities.”


c. Finally, I seek access to any communications exchanged between the AHBs responsible for owning/managing the aforementioned vacant units, and your Council's Housing Section, that pertain to the vacant units. 

The timeframe I am referring to for these communications is from 2020 to the present.

Applying this general public interest in transparency to the records at issue here, it is clear that the public interest is
served where the process of judicial appointments is made as transparent as possible. It is not just the fact that
judges are paid from public funds but more important perhaps is the fact that they are entrusted, on behalf of the
people, with independent and far-reaching powers. Furthermore, there is the reality that the process
of judicial appointments lacks innate transparency and that, outside of the limited scope of FOI, there is very little
by way of effective transparency mechanisms.

2. Residency Requirement Criteria (180-Day Rule)
• Minutes, reports, or correspondence discussing the establishment of the 180-day residency requirement for scheme eligibility.
• Assessments evaluating the psychological, emotional, and financial impact of this residency rule on survivors who were excluded due to shorter stays.
• Internal communications or legal opinions regarding the decision to exclude individuals based on the 180-day threshold, and whether alternative criteria were considered.
3. Institutional Reclassification & Exclusion of Survivors
• A list of institutions that were initially classified as Mother and Baby Homes or Children’s Homes but were later reclassified as Nursing Homes or other facilities.
• Internal records discussing the reclassification of these homes and the impact on survivors’ eligibility for redress.
• Justifications or discussions regarding the exclusion of survivors who were in these institutions as children but were later deemed ineligible because the facility was reclassified.
• Any legal or policy advice given to the government on this matter.
4. Consultation Process & Survivor Feedback
• Records of consultations held with survivors or advocacy groups regarding the 180-day requirement and the exclusion of certain institutions.
• Documentation showing how survivor feedback was considered in the final decision-making process.
5. Additional Questions on Scheme Development
• Minutes of all meetings held by the Interdepartmental Group concerning the development of the Restorative Recognition Scheme from its establishment to the present date.
• Correspondence (emails, letters, or memos) exchanged between your department and other government bodies regarding the Restorative Recognition Scheme.
• Reports, proposals, or cost analyses prepared by or submitted to the IDG relating to the development and implementation of the scheme.
• Details of any financial allocations or budgets assigned to the scheme by your department, including any projected costs and payments made to date.
• Any legal advice or assessments received by your department regarding the exclusion of certain survivors from the scheme.
• Internal communications, policy discussions, or decisions regarding the refusal to conduct an excavation of Sean Ross Abbey or other Mother and Baby Home sites.
• A list of individuals, organisations, or external consultants who were involved in advising or assisting with the scheme.
6. Costing and Financial Valuation of Trauma in the Restorative Recognition Scheme
• Records outlining how the financial compensation amounts were determined for survivors in the scheme.
• Any economic assessments, cost-benefit analyses, or internal discussions on how to put a monetary value on trauma and suffering experienced by survivors.
• Minutes, reports, or correspondence regarding the decision-making process for setting the payment amounts based on length of stay.
• Any external consultants or research studies referenced when deciding on the financial compensation structure.
• Documentation of whether individual psychological or financial impact assessments were considered when deciding payment amounts.

7. Disparity Between Industrial School Redress and Mother and Baby Home Redress
• Records detailing why survivors of Industrial Schools received higher financial redress payments compared to survivors of Mother and Baby Homes.
• Documentation explaining why no minimum residency period applied to Industrial School survivors, but a 180-day requirement was imposed on Mother and Baby Home survivors.
• Any internal discussions, correspondence, or legal advice on how redress amounts were determined for each category of survivor (Mother and Baby Homes vs. Industrial Schools).
• Reports or assessments comparing the impact of institutional abuse in Industrial Schools vs. Mother and Baby Homes, and how that was factored into payment calculations.
• A list of officials or decision-makers responsible for setting these different payment structures and criteria.
8. Accountability of Interdepartmental Group (IDG) Members
• Records detailing the professional backgrounds, qualifications, and relevant expertise (particularly in trauma, psychology, or child welfare) of each member of the Interdepartmental Group.
• Any records discussing the selection process for these individuals and why they were chosen.
• Minutes or records showing each member’s contributions to discussions on:
- The 180-day exclusion rule.
- The financial valuation of trauma.
- The decision not to include certain institutions (e.g., reclassified children’s homes).
- The lack of excavation at Mother and Baby Home sites.
• Any internal disagreements or objections raised by members regarding these decisions.
• Any communications between these individuals and external consultants, legal advisors, or government officials about the scheme.
• Any records of political or legal advice received on how to structure redress payments and exclusions.
9. Involvement of Religious Orders in the Restorative Recognition Scheme
• Records of meetings, correspondence, or discussions between government departments and religious orders (such as the Sisters of the Sacred Hearts of Jesus and Mary, the Good Shepherd Sisters, the Sisters of Mercy, etc.) regarding their financial or other contributions to the redress scheme.
• Any legal advice, discussions, or negotiations about holding religious institutions accountable for financial compensation to survivors.

My request relates to the DPMA allowance. On Feb 1, 2023 the then Taoiseach, Leo Varadkar, took Leaders' Questions and addressed issues related to the withholding of the DPMA allowance from certain individuals in care.  https://www.oireachtas.ie/en/debates/debate/dail/2023-02-01/10/
He said:
In 1996, the allowance was renamed the disability allowance and responsibility for it was transferred to the Department of Social, Community and Family Affairs, as it was called at the time.
Since 2007, it has been paid in full to people with disabilities living in long-term care, so this matter was resolved 15 years ago. However, the question that arose in 2009 was whether there should have been retrospection and back pay. It is an historical issue, a legacy issue, but to me it does appear different from the nursing homes charges issue. It appears different in substance because the legal advice is different and the legal advice and position became clearer after the High Court ruling. It is something we are going to look into over the next week or two and respond to further.
And the legal advice on the DPMA was that the State did not have a leg to stand on.
Over the course of the next few days comments from other ministers discussed potential restitution and other options.
I seek: All correspondence and documents on the issue regarding the assessment, discussion or resolution of this issue. This should include any details on measures proposed or tabled to address this matter and any memo that went to the Taoiseach's office on this issue.
For the avoidance of doubt, the purpose of this request is to establish what actions were taken or considered to address this. My request can be limited to any document created or circulated after January 28, 2023.
The request is focused on the DPMA issue and not the similar nursing home issue that was also discussed in the debate.

Galway City Council recently implemented an "upgrade" of the Kirwan Roundabout (intersection of N6 and N84), converting it to a signalised junction. Such schemes require a Road Safety Audit, which is to be done in stages as the project advances from planning, through design to actual works and eventual use by the public. According to TII: Road Safety Audit (RSA) is to be carried out on all new national road infrastructure projects and on all schemes which result in a permanent change to the existing road or roadside layout. RSA is carried out at different stages of an infrastructure project. RSA is a check for safety issues within a scheme rather than an identification of non-compliance with design standards. During RSA the audit team looks at the scheme from the point of view of all road users, with particular attention being paid to the needs of vulnerable road users. The RSA team identifies potential safety problems within the scheme and makes recommendations to the designer to minimise future collision occurrence and severity. meeting, given the range of themes and issues to be considered in this evolving
area. The document should include consideration of any implications that the new
EU Standards for Equality Bodies may have in respect of these matters when they
come into force. Barry Price left the meeting.

service includes not only the level and quality of service given to our customers but also the quality
of our decision-making processes, the efficiency and effectiveness of our corporate operations,
standard of our facilities and our ability to adapt in an ever-changing environment.
To provide the most effective and targeted range of services to meet the needs of the citizens,

Can you appeal against the decision?

rows: Access to Information on the Environment
European Communities (Access to Information on the Environment) Regulations 2007 to
2011 (S.I. No. 133 of 2007 and S.I. No. 662 of 2011) (hereafter referred to as the AIE
Regulations), give legal rights to those seeking to access information on the environment
from public authorities. Under these regulations, information relating to the environment
held by, or for, a public authority must be made available on request, subject to certain
exceptions. The AIE Regulations provide a definition of environmental information; outlines
the way requests for information may be submitted to public authorities and the way public
authorities are required to deal with requests.

or electronic form; provide your contact details; state, in terms that are as specific as

specific format or manner of access, you should specify this in your request.

rows: County Councils were established under the Local Government (Ireland) Act 1898. The first meeting of King’s (Offaly)
County Council was held on 22nd April 1899 in the Grand Jury Rooms, Courthouse, Tullamore. Laois and Offaly were
grouped together under the City and County Management Act 1940.  At the May Monthly Council Meeting in 1981 the
members supported a motion that the two counties should cease to be grouped in accordance with the provisions of
Section 13 of the City and County Management (Amendment) Act 1955. Since 2001, Offaly County Council has had its
headquarters at Áras an Chontae Charleville Road, Tullamore.
Offaly County Council is an organisation of more than 350 staff. Offaly County Council is both a provider of essential
services to the citizens of Offaly as well as a representational body for the people of Offaly. Local Government in Ireland
operates jointly through directly elected representatives and full time executives headed by the Chief Executive,
Ms. Anna Marie Delaney was appointed Chief Executive to Offaly County Council in February 2016.
The Chief Executive (CE) of the Council is responsible for the day to day operations of Offaly County Council. She acts
by means of a written Chief Executive’s Order. When making decisions the CE must act in a way that is consistent with
the policy framework that has been established by the elected members and she must take into account the wishes of
the elected members. The CE has delegated her powers, duties and functions in relation to a number of service areas
to individual members of the Senior Management Team which is made up of Directors of Service and Head of Finance
in a number of different departments within the Council.

he purpose of this procedures manual is to provide guidance for staff in relation to the conduct
of reviews by the Information Commissioner2 under section 22 of the Freedom of Information

to dealing with reviews.  The procedures set out in this manual should, in the normal course of
events, be adhered to insofar as is practicable.  It should be noted, however, that the FOI Act
provides that the Commissioner has discretion to adopt such procedures as are appropriate in all
the circumstances of a case.  It is also relevant to note that the Commissioner’s review functions
are inquisitorial and generally informal rather than adversarial in nature.  In all circumstances,

whether there is a reasonable possibility of resolving the case without issuing a binding

withdrawal has a number of advantages.  From an applicant’s point of view, settlement or
withdrawal can result in a speedier resolution of the matter and a refund of the
application fee.  From the point of view of the FOI body, granting access to the records in
question can avoid the need for any further time consuming written submissions; for
instance, where consideration of the request for focused submissions reveals that the
body had misdirected itself in its decision.
In endeavouring to reach a settlement, Investigating Officers should make it clear that
settlement is not an exercise designed to reduce the rights of applicants in any way.
Rather, it is a process which is aimed at narrowing the differences between the sides.  In
some cases, a point is reached at which the applicant is happy to accept the decision of
the FOI body as modified in the course of the settlement procedure.  In other cases,
differences remain which can only be resolved by way of a binding decision of the
Commissioner.  Where the FOI body agrees to release a significant amount of additional
records, the Investigating Officer should confirm interest before proceedings (in
reference to section 22(9)(a)(iv) or (v) of the Act, if appropriate).  Even if a binding
decision is required, the settlement process can help to ensure that the decision
concentrates only on the essentials of the dispute between the parties.
In any case where the Investigating Officer considers that there is a possibility of settling
the case or narrowing the differences between the parties, s/he should contact the parties
concerned, using informal methods of communication wherever possible (e.g., telephone
call followed by brief email), and outline the possible basis of the settlement.  In
considering the possibility for settlement, regard should be had not alone to granting
access to the records at issue, but also to the possibilities that a different form of access

be acceptable.  The possibility of settlement should be considered in section 38 cases,

As submissions made by one or more parties to a review are likely to contain sensitive
information that may not be appropriate for disclosure to others, submissions are not
exchanged as a general rule.  In particular, care must be taken that the provisions of
section 25(3) of the FOI Act are fully observed.  Section 25(3) requires the
Commissioner to take all reasonable precautions to prevent the disclosure of information
contained in an exempt record or information which if included in a record would cause
the record to be an exempt record, or information as to whether a record does or does not
exist where the FOI body is required by the Act not to disclose this information.  Any
exception to the rule against the exchange of submissions requires the consent of the
relevant parties and the prior approval of the relevant Senior Investigator.
An Investigating Officer should, however, notify the relevant party or parties to a review,
preferably by email, of new material issues arising for consideration insofar as they affect
the interests of the party or parties concerned.  Material issues are issues that are relevant
to the outcome of the review. Such issues involve information of significance (i.e. of
substance and importance) that is likely to influence the decision the Commissioner will
make, i.e. information that will make a difference to the outcome of the review. Where
the influence of new material issues is likely to be adverse to a party to a review, the
party concerned should be given notice of the matter and an opportunity to respond. In
other words, any new matter of which a party to a review is unaware and which is likely
to cause the Commissioner to make a decision adverse to the interests of that party should
be communicated to the party concerned.  Such matters would generally include
applicable exemptions not previously raised, pertinent search details not previously
disclosed to the applicant, and any new facts and new legal developments which are
likely to have a significant bearing on the outcome of the review.
The notification need not necessarily be detailed and should be given by informal means
wherever possible, but the applicant should be made aware of the pertinent factual
matters under consideration, particularly where and insofar as these matters are likely to
cause the Commissioner to affirm the decision of the FOI body. By the same token, the
FOI body or, where relevant, affected third party should be given notice where a new
matter of relevance arises that is likely to result in a decision to direct release of the
records concerned. (For the sake of clarity, please note that this would not include a
simple failure of proof or conclusions drawn having regard to the contents of the records
at issue.  Furthermore, it would not include an explanation of how the Commissioner
interprets and applies the exemptions claimed.)
Thus, for instance, if an applicant who has been notified of new material issues arising
from the FOI body’s submissions raises pertinent factual matters in turn which appear to
undermine the FOI body’s case for exemption, the FOI body should be given an
opportunity to respond before a decision is made.  If, on the other hand, the applicant
simply argues against the case made by the FOI body without identifying new material
facts for consideration, the matter should be ready for decision even where the applicant’s
arguments are persuasive or the proposed decision is otherwise in the applicant’s favour
(subject of course to any required notification of affected third parties).
As new claims for exemption are likely to involve new matters of relevance, these too
should generally be notified to the applicant. The need for notification can arise even
within an exemption category. For instance, a claim of trade secrets can differ
substantially from a claim of mere prejudice to the competitive position of a company.
Thus, where a general claim for exemption under section 36 has been made, it may be
necessary to notify the applicant once the basis for the claim is identified by the FOI body
or the affected third party. The same may be true for a claim of prejudice to
investigations v. a claim of a significant, adverse effect on the performance of a
management function in relation to a refusal under section 30(1) of the Act.
However, where the FOI body has identified all material facts that are relevant to more
than one ground for refusal, such as an exemption and also a restriction involving the
remit of the Act, it may not be necessary to put an applicant on notice that an alternative
ground for refusal than the one referred to by the FOI body will be applied by the
Commissioner. Thus, for instance, where the FOI body has refused access to a record
under section 31(1)(a) on the basis that it contains legal advice provided by the Office of
the Attorney General, it should not be necessary to notify the applicant before a decision
is made finding that the record actually falls within the ambit of section 42(f) because it
was created by the Office of the Attorney General and is not a record relating to general
administration.   Where an Investigating Officer is satisfied that no new material issues
arise, or that the applicant has had an adequate opportunity to make submissions
addressing the material issues arising in the case, s/he may make a recommendation to
the Commissioner without further reference to the applicant.
Determining the materiality of an issue, as well as the level of detail that may be required,

contexts, but it nevertheless can be difficult to know what is truly “material” unless and

have regard to our Values and Behaviours Framework, on the one hand, and the need for
expediency (section 22(3) refers) and the requirements of section 25(3) on the other.

Seeking clarification in cases proceeding to decision is required when certain gaps must
or should be addressed in order to remove an element of uncertainty or confusion in
relation to material matters.  The need for clarification typically arises when a prima facie
case for exemption appears to have been made, but certain details are missing that are
required in order for the Commissioner to give adequate reasons for affirming the refusal
of access.  Thus, for instance, where the records involve technical or complex
information, clarification may be required in order to gain a better understanding of the
subject matter or to distinguish the information at issue from other similar information
that may appear to be available from other sources.  It may also be necessary to check on
the status of certain time-bound events that are relevant to a claim for exemption, for
instance, whether a certain investigation or court proceedings remain ongoing.
As a general rule, a period of no longer than two weeks should be allowed for providing
the clarification sought.  Where the element of uncertainty or confusion is not adequately
addressed in the period allowed, the Investigating Officer may need to reconsider any
conclusions that may have tentatively been drawn regarding the claims made for
exemption.  The Investigating Officer should not, however, continue to engage in
correspondence over the matter without the approval of a Senior Investigator (who may
determine that a section 45 notice is warranted or that the matter is ready to be brought to
conclusion subject to any further notifications that may be required).
Where the FOI body falls short of establishing a prima facie case for exemption in the

seeking clarification is distinct from the requirement to notify parties of new material
Further submissions, made for whatever purpose, may give rise to further queries, but
there are limits to any investigation.  While the Commissioner’s review is inquisitorial in
nature, it is not the role of the Investigating Officer to determine beyond a reasonable
doubt whether the decision of the FOI body was correct or not.  Rather, the question for
determination is whether it has been shown to the satisfaction of the Commissioner that
the decision of the FOI body was justified or not. Section 22(3) requires the
Commissioner to determine this question as soon as may be and, in so far as practicable,
not later than 4 months after the receipt of the application for the review concerned.
What is required is evidence that is sufficient in all of the circumstances. Therefore,
further enquiries should be made only where necessary and with the approval of the
Investigating Officer’s Manager. However, the Investigating Officer and his/her Manager
must be satisfied that the Commissioner has sufficient information on which to make a
decision and that all relevant information before the Commissioner is given due
consideration. Moreover, any uncertainty over material issues of fact must be adequately
resolved if these are to be relied upon in any finding in the Commissioner’s decision.
In conducting reviews, Investigating Officers must of course adhere to fair procedures.
However, the requirements of procedural fairness will depend upon the particular
circumstances of the case.  Where a question arises as to whether procedural fairness
requires further engagement with a party or parties, the Investigating Officer should
consult with his or her Manager so as to determine the appropriate course of action.

Any case closed by decision should be given a rating of 1, 2, or 3. A rating of 1 applies if

3.5.5  An FOI body may claim that a record never existed.  In some cases, it may be more the
circumstances of the case, rather than the searches carried out, that are most relevant.
Example:  In Case 160417 we found that a decision by St James’s Hospital to refuse the
applicant's request was justified on the basis that no relevant records existed.  The
applicant had been informed by the Hospital that access to medical treatment by a doctor
in the UK (Dr X) was not possible as Dr X no longer worked for the NHS.  The applicant
sought access to records relating to a telephone conversation which he believed took
place between Dr X/his secretary and a staff member of the Hospital.  The Hospital
informed us that it had written to Dr X requesting an assessment of the applicant and as
no reply was received, the Hospital's Medical Director conducted an internet search and
concluded from the result of the search that Dr X no longer worked for the NHS. The
Hospital maintained that there was no telephone call and, accordingly, no records within
the scope of the applicant's request.  It stated that the applicant's file had been searched
and that there was no record relating to contact with Dr X by the Hospital other than the
letter to Dr X which had already been released to him.  We affirmed the decision of the
Hospice stated that significant costs would be involved in carrying out such works. In the
circumstances, we did not consider it reasonable to expect the Hospice to undertake these
steps in relation to the applicant's request.
Example # 2:  In Case 180050 the applicant stated that he did not receive copies of
certain, specific emails between the Irish Greyhound Board (IGB) and the Department of
Agriculture, Food and the Marine on certain dates in 2013 that he believed to exist.  The
IGB stated that its email systems were updated in November 2013, which involved
"back-up" of its system, transferring from a tape based system to a "cloud" environment.
It stated that, as a result, only the electronic records of staff working with the IGB at that
time migrated to the new system and therefore its records prior to November 2013 were
incomplete. It stated that back up tapes existed containing the records of former staff.
However, it submitted that external assistance would be required to access material on the
tapes. According to the IGB, the likely cost of doing so on a per tape basis would have
been prohibitive, notwithstanding subsequent issues surrounding identification of any
relevant information held on the tapes. It seemed to us that there was no way of knowing
definitively whether relevant information would be identified if such measures were
taken. In the circumstances of this case, we found that it was not reasonable to require the
IGB to access information held on the tapes.

Example:  In Case 130242 the records the subject of the review were created by staff at a

removal, we considered the possibility that records which were the subject of an FOI

of the FOI body of higher rank than the person who made the initial decision.  This contrasts
with reviews by the Information Commissioner which are external to the FOI body.

I
nvestigations Unit – A unit staffed by AP/Investigators who report directly to a Senior
Investigator.  The unit processes cases, generally in “date of receipt” order, which are not
deemed suitable for immediate processing by the Assessment Unit, usually because of the
complex issues or large number of records involved.

P
erson to whom section 38(2) applies - In the case of a request for records which contain
information obtained in confidence, the person who gave the information to the FOI body, and, if
the head considers it appropriate, the person to whom the information relates.  In the case of a
request for records which contain personal information or commercially sensitive information,
the person to whom the information relates.

P
olicy Section – Established to develop guidance for Investigating Officers on the provisions of
Request to which section 38 relates - A request for access to records which contain information
obtained in confidence, commercially sensitive information or personal information where the
FOI body has formed the view (subject only to receiving the views of the party who gave the
information to the FOI body and/or a party to whom the information relates) that the public
interest would, on balance, be better served by granting than by refusing to grant the request.

R
equester - A person who makes a request to an FOI body under the FOI Act.  A requester to an
FOI body may become an applicant to the Office of the Information Commissioner.

S
ection 9 application - Section 9 of the FOI Act provides a right of amendment of personal
information relating to an individual contained in a record held by an FOI body where the
information is incomplete, incorrect or misleading.

S
ection 10 application - Section 10 of the FOI Act entitles a person who is affected by an act of
an FOI body and who has a material interest in a matter either affected by that act or to which
that act relates to request a statement of the reasons for the act and any findings on any material
issues of fact made for the purpose of the act.

S
ection 38 - Section 38 provides for a formal notification procedure whenever an FOI body is
considering the release of information obtained in confidence, commercially sensitive
information or personal information in the public interest.  It requires the FOI body to notify the
person who gave the information to the FOI body, and, if the FOI body considers it appropriate,
the person to whom the information relates, of the request and that the request falls to be granted
in the public interest. Any person so notified may then make submissions to the FOI body which
must be considered before deciding whether to grant or refuse access.

S
upport Unit - The unit which provides administrative support to Investigating Officers and

present that relate to unidentified aerial phenomena (UAP) and any associated physical,
geological, marine, or geophysical anomalies.

To assist with the practical handling of this request, I have set out below the specific record
types and systems I believe are most relevant, along with targeted search terms and filters that
may be used to identify responsive material.
1. INFOMAR and INSS Marine Survey Records
Materials to be searched:
• Sidescan sonar logs
• Multibeam bathymetry annotations
• Sub-bottom profiler records
• Marine anomaly registers
• Interpretive reports from mapping missions
Suggested search terms:
• “unidentified submerged object” or “USO”
• “non-acoustic sonar return”
• “object – no match to wreck database”
• “unusual sonar shadow”
• “transient sonar contact”
• “metallic return – unknown source”
2. Geophysical and Magnetic Anomaly Records

Materials to be searched:
• Magnetic anomaly maps
• Gravity survey records
• Electromagnetic disturbance reports
Suggested search terms:
• “localized magnetic spike”
• “EM field disruption”
• “magnetic signature – no geological match”
• “compass deviation”
• “short-duration high-field anomaly”
3. Irish National Seismic Network (ISNN) Data
Materials to be searched:
• Seismic event logs and waveforms
• Bulletins referencing non-tectonic events
• Internal memos explaining seismic data with no geophysical source
Suggested search terms:
• “airburst-like seismic event”

• “non-seismic waveform”
• “high-altitude source”
• “pressure signal unexplained”
• “sonic boom with no aircraft confirmed”
4. Duty Geologist Logs and Public Queries
Materials to be searched:
• Email logs at duty.geologist@gsi.ie
• Public query summaries
• Field reports following site visits
Suggested search terms:
• “burned soil” or “scorched vegetation”
• “circular ground impression”
• “trace evidence of aerial object”
• “soil radiation spike”
• “unusual plant growth”
• “metal fragment reported by public”

5. Geochemical and Physical Sample Analysis Records
Materials to be searched:
• Lab test reports (mineralogical, spectrographic, elemental)
• Unclassified sample investigations
• Communications with other agencies regarding unidentified material
Suggested search terms:
• “sample origin unknown”
• “non-standard alloy”
• “metallic fragment – not natural”
• “high-purity magnesium”
• “fused metal / slag – unidentified source”
• “microsphere analysis”
6. Internal and Interagency Correspondence
Materials to be searched:
• Email archives of staff in marine, geophysics, and minerals sections
• Memos and meeting notes involving anomaly reporting

• Correspondence with other state bodies (e.g. Defence Forces, Marine Institute, Met
Éireann)
Suggested search terms:
• “UAP”
• “UFO”
• “unidentified aerial”
• “radar contact unexplained”
• “Defence Forces query – aerial object”
• “interagency meeting – UAP”

The term "flight path" is not a defined legal or technical term in Irish aviation or planning law. Its use by daa conflates
separate processes:
- The Standard Instrument Departure (SID) is an Instrument Flight Procedure assessed for navigational safety by the Irish
Aviation Authority (IAA);
- The route actually flown by aircraft, including turn points and headings, is what has environmental and planning
significance - and what was subject to assessment in the planning process
This request does not seek information about generic SID design or ICAO compliance. It seeks to understand:
- Whether/when officials within the Department of Transport knew what route is actually being flown from Runway 28R;
- Whether/when officials within the Department of Transport authorised that route;
- Whether/when officials within the Department of Transport were aware that this route deviates from the one assessed
and approved in the 2007 EIS Request:

Further to my 3 x FOI requests submitted to XXXX in July 2021 (attached) I am advised by the OIC
that Section 11.9 of the act applies.
As you will know, Section 11.9 states that '...a record in the possession of a service provider shall, if
and in so far as it relates to the service, be deemed for the purposes of this Act to be held by the FOI
body, and there shall be deemed to be included in the contract for the service a provision that the
service provider shall, if so requested by the FOI body for the purposes of this Act, give the record to
the FOI body for retention by it for such period as is reasonable in the particular circumstances ....'
The OIC further advised me that '... For the purposes of the Act, a service provider means a person
who, at the time the request was made, was not an FOI body but was providing a service for an FOI
body under a contract for services, including an administrative arrangement between the parties....'
Given that the department has a Service Level Agreement (attached) with XXXX there can be no
disputing that XXXX is providing a service for an FOI body (DAFM). Therefore I request that the
department gather the records from XXXX and process them in accordance with the act.

1. Internal departmental correspondence in relation to Parliamentary question 50300/23 from
Patrick Costello here (below) “Deputy Patrick Costello asked the Tánaiste and Minister for
Foreign Affairs if his Department is carrying out checks at Shannon Airport on US military
vehicles which are stopping off enroute to Israel and other jurisdictions; if so, the number that
have taken place in the past ten years; and if he will make a statement on the matter.
[50300/23]”
2. Internal departmental correspondence in relation to Parliamentary question 50512/23 from
Matt Carthy here (below) “Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign
Affairs the steps he has taken to ensure that military aircraft of foreign states landing in
Ireland or overflights in sovereign Irish airspace are unarmed, carry no arms, ammunition or
explosives and do not engage in intelligence gathering or form part of military exercises or
operations; and whether there has been any review of the oversight of these matters in the
context of the Israeli military assaults on Gaza. [50512/23]”
3. Any documents related to any consultation between the Department of Foreign Affairs and
the Department of Transport and/or the Department of Justice to determine if there are
foreign policy or security considerations to take into account for the five most recent requests
for exemptions in respect of munitions of war as indicated by the Minister here (below) “I
have addressed the wider issues relating to Ireland’s approach to the current crisis in Israel
and the occupied Palestinian territory on frequent occasions over recent weeks so I will focus
my response on issues relating to diplomatic clearance for military aircraft. Under the terms of
the Air Navigation (Foreign Military Aircraft) Order, 1952, all foreign military aircraft wishing to
overfly, or land in, the State require diplomatic clearance from the Minister for Foreign Affairs.
Diplomatic clearance is subject to strict conditions, including that the aircraft is unarmed; that
it carries no arms, ammunition or explosives; that it does not engage in intelligence gathering;
and that the flight in question does not form part of a military exercise or operation. This
policy is well known and is fully understood by the United States and other international
partners, and is done in compliance with Ireland’s traditional policy of military neutrality. With
regard to the transit of US military aircraft through Shannon and other Irish airports, the
Department of Foreign Affairs publishes statistics in relation to overflights and landings of
foreign military and state aircraft on the Department’s website. This includes details on the

number of US military aircraft that have landed in Shannon airport this year. My Department
is committed to the highest standards of transparency and, as such, will continue to publish
details relating to overflights and landings on a monthly basis on the Department’s website, as
well as working to compile and publish historic data relating to overflights and landing of
foreign military aircraft where and when possible.”

PART 1 – FORMAL REQUEST FOR REVERSAL OF DECISION NOT TO HOLD AN ORAL HEARING
1. Inconsistency With the Planning and Development Act 2000 and ABP Guidelines

Under Section 37O and Section 134 of the Planning and Development Act 2000 (as amended), the Board holds the discretion to convene an oral hearing where necessary to ensure a fair assessment of the application, or where issues of significance and

complexity arise. Your own criteria for oral hearings state that they are appropriate where: - significant public concern exists, - complex environmental or technical issues arise, - further clarification is in the public interest, - or the nature and scale of the
development warrant oral examination. This proposal meets all such criteria.

2. Direct Precedent: A Nearly Identical Application Previously Received an Oral Hearing - A previous Bord na Móna application of almost identical scale, location, and design for the same general area was granted a full Oral Hearing and was ultimately

refused on the basis of the evidence examined there. It is impossible to reconcile the current decision with the approach taken previously for: - the same developer, - the same geographical area, - similar environmental impacts, - identical community
concerns, - and the same technical questions.

3. Extremely Poor Community Engagement by Bord na Móna - Bord na Móna has failed to meet any reasonable interpretation of meaningful community engagement. Only a single-page generic letter was issued to residents; the developer did not attend

local meetings, did not host information sessions, and did not provide any forum for local concerns to be raised. This falls below standards required by: - national Wind Energy Development Guidelines, - Aarhus Convention principles, - and best practice

for major infrastructure developments. Given the developer’s complete failure to engage with the local community, an oral hearing is the only remaining mechanism through which the public can participate meaningfully.
4. Scale, Impact, and Complexity Strongly Favour an Oral Hearing

This proposal involves: - 22 turbines, - a 110kV substation, - extensive new access roads, - major environmental, hydrological, landscape, noise, and biodiversity impacts. Such issues are precisely those for which oral hearings exist, providing the
essential opportunity to question expert evidence and clarify technical matters.

5. Determining the Application on Written Submissions Alone Would Contravene Principles of Fairness and Natural Justice - Given the scale of impact, the lack of community engagement, the technical complexity, and the precedent of a previous oral

hearing for the same site, proceeding without an oral hearing would raise serious concerns regarding transparency and procedural fairness. I therefore request that An Coimisiún Pleanála reverse its decision of 25 November 2025 and convene a full

I wish to request access to any analysis of / report on FOI activity in 2025 in your FOI body.
​I am seeking any single record, or the smallest number of records possible to provide the information sought - I am not seeking "any and all" such
records.

​I would like to request the following information in accordance with the aforementioned legislation as a Freedom of Information request or as a
request for access to information on the environment, whichever is most appropriate in the circumstances; the number of books in the library that
were disposed of in tabular form from 2020-2024 inclusive; the cost of the book disposal for that period; the name of the disposal contractor for this
purpose from 2020-2024. ​

​I am writing to you to seek information and records from the 1st January 2020 up to the 31st December 2024, in tabular form, pursuant to
the Freedom of Information Act 2014, and the European Regulations (Access to Information on the Environment) 2007–2018 (AIE Regulations)
Unless otherwise stated, this request relates the the period:
Information and Records requested
Dog Pound Intake, Results and Statistics
For evert dog pound under the care of the Local Authority, on a yearly basis:
* The total number of creatures taken in
*The various catagories of creatures taken in
* The number of creatures returned to owners
* The number of creatures relocated (including transfers to welfare charities or organisations)
* The number of creatures put down
* The number of creatures who died in the care of the Authority (not including being put down)
* The average and maximum length of stay
* Breakdown according to age catagory (where it was recorded) and according to reason for intake (e.g. stray, seized, given up)
* The pound welfare policies, standard operating procedures, or guidelines
* The frequency of vet visits.
* Records of disease outbreaks, injuries or animal/staff welfare incidents
* The number of inspections of the pound made by the Local Authority or third parties.
* Correspondance relating to the Dog Breeding Establishments Act 2010, the Animal Health and Welfare Act 2013, or other related regulations.
* The number of reports in which deficiences, remedial actions, or improvements needed or implements are recognised
Under the AIE Regulation, I am seeking records relating to the environmental aspects of pound operations, including:
*The waste management policy, including disposal of animal remains and vet waste
* Biosecurity and disease control policy
* Environmental assessments, reports or correspondance regarding pound facilities
* Records of incidents or complaints relating to environmental impact
Contracts, Procurement and Costs
* Contracts, service level agreements or procurement records relating to dog pound operation by private contractors
* Costs incurred by the Local Authority by operating or outsourcing dog pound services
* Payments made to third party operators or welfare organisations
Complaints, Enforcement and Oversight
* Records or complaints received by the council and/or the pound regarding animal welfare
* Records of enforcement, investigation or prosecution actions relating to dog pound operations.

​I am seeking the following:​The number of applications for homeless services made to the council, by year, for each of the years 2016 to 2025; the
number of approved applications for homeless services made to the council, by year, for each of the years 2016 to 2025; and the number of rejected
applications for homeless services made to the council, by year, for each of the years 2016 to 2025.

I am writing under the Freedom of Information Act 2014 to request the following records from the Roads Department:
Any correspondence with Coolmore Stud, its owners, or any employees, agents or representatives of Coolmore Stud or its owners, regarding the N24
Waterford to Cahir, from January 1st, 2020 to present.

​I wish to request access to all records relating to the full cost associated with the Part 8 Site Remediation Works at Ballypadeen, Cashel, Co. Tipperary, including
but not limited to the following:
1. Total projected cost of the remediation worksAll estimates, costings, budgets, tenders, consultant reports, engineering assessments, or internal financial
projections relating to the proposed remediation works.
2. All costs incurred to dateAny expenditure already incurred in relation to the Ballypadeen site, including: Environmental assessmentsEngineering reportsConsultant
feesLegal feesContractor or preparatory worksSite investigationsAny other related expenditure
3. Insurance coverage and liabilityRecords confirming whether any portion of the remediation costs will be covered by Tipperary County Council's insurers.Records
showing: Whether the insurer has accepted or declined liability for remediation costsAny excess, deductible, or contribution payable by the CouncilAny
correspondence with insurers relating to the remediation works
4. Funding sourceRecords identifying whether the remediation works will be funded: Fully by Tipperary County CouncilPartially by insurersThrough central
government grantsThrough any other funding mechanism
5. Internal communicationsAny internal memos, emails, reports, or briefings discussing the financial implications of the remediation works.
6. Consideration of retrofit, partial remediation, or phased completion
Please provide all records, reports, assessments, engineering advice, consultant recommendations, internal memos, or financial analyses that consider:Retrofit or
partial remediation of the Ballypadeen sitePhased or staged completion of the works rather than full remediation in a single projectAny cost–benefit analysis,
feasibility study, or comparative costing between: full remediation,partial remediation,retrofit options,staged/phased works, orany other alternative options
considered by the Council or its consultants
This includes any records that discuss whether such options were considered, evaluated, rejected, or deemed feasible or infeasible.
Request for Urgency
I request that this FOI application be processed as a matter of urgency.
There is an active Part 8 public consultation underway for the Ballypadeen Site Remediation Works. For members of the public to make informed, meaningful
submissions, it is essential that the full financial implications of the proposed works, including all costings, funding sources, and alternative options, are available
before the consultation period closes.
The information sought is directly relevant to:the public's ability to understand the scale and justification of the proposed works,the financial impact on public funds,
andthe evaluation of whether alternative, less costly approaches were considered.
Delaying release until after the consultation period would undermine the purpose of public participation and would not align with the principles of transparency and
accountability set out in Section 11(3) of the FOI Act.
For these reasons, I respectfully request that the Council expedite processing of this request

I am researching Council procedures, regarding missing drawings in a planning permission obtained in !973,
Please confirm the exact procedure of your Council to resolve a problem with a historical planning permission granted in 1973. Permission was
granted for a private dwelling and is confirmed in writing. No objections were made by either the Council or the public and the dwelling was built. No
modifications have been made since 1973.
The drawings in the planning file are NOT the drawings submitted by the applicant in 1973. They do not contain the Applicants name, address, date or
a scale of the drawings as required to issue a planning permission at the time.There is no Architect name on the drawings so it is not possible to
contact that company. The drawings on file are generic but are not site specific.
We, as present owners, are requesting that the Council confirm the house as built did have planning permission. Mediation is also offered by us to
resolve as the correct drawings have obviously been mislaid by the council. What is the procedure of your council if this situation arose ?
The query is not for a file in your Council. I merely wish to establish what is the procedure if such a problem arose in your Council area.
If you are unable to confirm the procedure in your Council please forward this request to the relevant person in the Council and advise me of
same.
The problem arose in another Local Authority who are now claiming that the planning permission obtained in 1973 is invalid and I must apply for
retention ( Quoted cost by Arch is 6,500) . I have queried the Planning Regulator and they have advised that this is not a SYSTEMIC problem / resolution
and I should take legal action against the local authority. This I don't want to do and therefore I am trying to see how other authorities would deal with
it.
​This is merely an information gathering exercise. Hope you can help as we are both in our seventies and don't have the 6,500 for a retention
application ( drawings etc). I would appreciate any advice you can give me.

This request relates to the Suir Blueway at Kilsheelan and the Council's position that the Blueway is recorded on the Council's Road Schedule as Road L-6516 and has
been declared a public road pursuant to the Roads Act 1993.

Kilsheelan. If required, I can provide an Eircode or marked-up map.
​Please provide copies of the following records held by Tipperary County Council (including attachments):
1) Declaration / legal instrument
All records comprising the decision, order or instrument by which the Suir Blueway (or the relevant section at Kilsheelan) was declared a public road under the Roads
Act 1993, including any schedules, maps or public notices.
2) Road Schedule and map – L-6516
The Road Schedule entry for Road L-6516 and the corresponding map(s) showing the precise route and extent at Kilsheelan (Roads Act 1993, s10(5)).
3) Mapped extent in usable format (GIS)
Any GIS/polyline/shapefile or other electronic mapping records used to represent Road L-6516 and/or the Suir Blueway in the Council's systems.
Pursuant to FOI Act 2014, s17 and s17(4), I request access in electronic form where held (for example: GIS export, PDF map extract, or screenshots of the relevant
layer with legend and scale).
4) Records defining extent, width, alignment and responsibility (Kilsheelan section only)
Any records that define or describe the legal extent, width or alignment of the route at Kilsheelan, including any taking-in-charge, vesting, wayleave or route-definition
documents, insofar as such records are relied upon to define Road L-6516 / the Suir Blueway.
5) Agreements affecting control of the route (Kilsheelan section only)
Any agreements or formal correspondence between Tipperary County Council and Waterways Ireland (or any other body) that define or affect the alignment, extent,
control or responsibility for the route at Kilsheelan.
Scope/time limit (to avoid unnecessary burden):
This request is limited to records currently in force and relied upon, and any earlier foundational instruments still relied upon, plus records created or updated in the
last 10 years insofar as they relate to the above.

process. Please also confirm the statutory decision date for this request
